name: rag_eval_45
description: 45 questions over three public pages (two encyclopedia articles and one technical documentation page). Types: fact (single detail), multi-part (several details) and unanswerable (the page does not contain the answer). Drafted with AI assistance; every evidence phrase was checked against the extracted page text.

cases.question: In what year was retrieval-augmented generation first proposed?
cases.expected_answer: It was first proposed in 2020.
evidence: first proposed in 2020
introduced in a 2020 paper

cases.question: What incorrect information did Google's Bard give in its first demonstration, and what did it cost Google?
cases.expected_answer: Bard gave incorrect information about the James Webb Space Telescope, contributing to a $100 billion decline in Google's stock value.
evidence: $100 billion decline

cases.question: What is the technique of adding relevant context to the user's input called?
cases.expected_answer: Prompt stuffing.
evidence: prompt stuffing

cases.question: Where are the embeddings stored so that documents can be retrieved?
cases.expected_answer: In a vector database.
evidence: stored in a vector database

cases.question: How do sparse vectors differ from dense vectors?
cases.expected_answer: Sparse vectors encode the identity of a word, are dictionary-length and mostly zeros; dense vectors encode meaning, are more compact and contain fewer zeros.
evidence: Sparse vectors, which encode the identity of a word

cases.question: What task can be used to pre-train the retriever?
cases.expected_answer: The Inverse Cloze Task (ICT), which has the model predict masked text within documents.
evidence: Inverse Cloze Task

cases.question: What is the more reproducible version of Retro called?
cases.expected_answer: Retro++, which includes in-context RAG.
evidence: is called Retro++

cases.question: What trade-off does chunk size involve?
cases.expected_answer: A trade-off between focused retrieval and contextual completeness: smaller chunks isolate relevant information but can omit context, while larger chunks keep context but may include irrelevant material and use more of the input budget.
evidence: trade-off between focused retrieval and contextual completeness

cases.question: How does hybrid search help when vector search misses key facts?
cases.expected_answer: It also runs a traditional full-text search and combines those results with the vector-search chunks before feeding them to the language model.
evidence: traditional text search

cases.question: Does RAG prevent hallucinations?
cases.expected_answer: No. RAG does not prevent hallucinations; the model can still hallucinate around the source material.
evidence: RAG does not prevent hallucinations

cases.question: What did the 2020 paper that introduced RAG combine?
cases.expected_answer: A parametric language model with a non-parametric external memory accessed through retrieval at inference time.
evidence: non-parametric external memory

cases.question: What are the common approaches to text chunking?
cases.expected_answer: Fixed-length, recursive and semantic chunking.
evidence: fixed-length, recursive and semantic chunking

cases.question: How do dot products and approximate nearest neighbor search each improve vector retrieval?
cases.expected_answer: Dot products enhance similarity scoring, while approximate nearest neighbor (ANN) searches improve retrieval efficiency over K-nearest neighbors (KNN) searches.
evidence: Dot products enhance similarity scoring

cases.question: How much does it cost per month to run a RAG system in production?
cases.expected_answer: The source does not contain enough information to answer this question.

cases.question: Which company released the first commercial RAG chatbot?
cases.expected_answer: The source does not contain enough information to answer this question.

cases.question: What other names are used for a vector database?
cases.expected_answer: A vector store or a vector search engine.
evidence: vector store or vector search engine

cases.question: What kind of algorithms do vector databases typically implement?
cases.expected_answer: Approximate nearest neighbor algorithms.
evidence: typically implement approximate nearest neighbor

cases.question: How many dimensions can vector embeddings have?
cases.expected_answer: From a few hundred to tens of thousands, depending on how complex the data is.
evidence: from a few hundred to tens of thousands

cases.question: What is the goal when computing feature vectors for data items?
cases.expected_answer: Semantically similar data items should receive feature vectors that are close to each other.
evidence: semantically similar data items receive feature vectors close to each other

cases.question: What are the common techniques for similarity search on high-dimensional vectors?
cases.expected_answer: HNSW graphs, locality-sensitive hashing (LSH) and sketching, product quantization (PQ), and inverted files.
evidence: Hierarchical Navigable Small World (HNSW) graphs

cases.question: Which implementations performed best in recent vector search benchmarks?
cases.expected_answer: HNSW-based implementations.
evidence: HNSW-based implementations have been among the best performers

cases.question: Which conferences have hosted competitions on vector search?
cases.expected_answer: SISAP (the International Conference on Similarity Search and Applications) and NeurIPS.
evidence: International Conference on Similarity Search and Applications (SISAP)

cases.question: What can vector retrieval be combined with to support hybrid retrieval?
cases.expected_answer: Metadata filtering, lexical or sparse retrieval, graph-based retrieval, and multimodal retrieval.
evidence: combined with metadata filtering

cases.question: How is the retrieval component of a RAG system most often implemented?
cases.expected_answer: As a vector database.
evidence: most often implemented as a vector database

cases.question: In RAG, what happens to the documents retrieved from the vector database?
cases.expected_answer: They are added into the context window of the large language model, which then writes a response.
evidence: added into the context window

cases.question: How does searching a vector database differ from looking up records in a traditional database?
cases.expected_answer: Vector databases find records that are semantically similar to the input, while traditional databases mainly look up records by exact match.
evidence: primarily look up records by exact match

cases.question: What does list.append() do?
cases.expected_answer: It adds an item to the end of the list.
evidence: add an item to the end of the list

cases.question: What exception does list.remove() raise when the value is not in the list?
cases.expected_answer: A ValueError.
evidence: raises a ValueError if there is no such item

cases.question: What does a.pop() return when no index is given?
cases.expected_answer: It removes and returns the last item in the list.
evidence: removes and returns the last item in the list

cases.question: What do list methods like insert, remove and sort return?
cases.expected_answer: Nothing useful: they modify the list in place and return the default None.
evidence: they return the default

cases.question: Why are lists not efficient for use as queues?
cases.expected_answer: Inserting or popping at the beginning is slow because all the other elements have to be shifted by one.
evidence: all of the other elements have to be shifted by one

cases.question: What should you use to implement a queue in Python?
cases.expected_answer: collections.deque, which has fast appends and pops from both ends.
evidence: designed to have fast appends and pops from both ends

cases.question: What does a list comprehension consist of?
cases.expected_answer: Brackets containing an expression followed by a for clause, then zero or more for or if clauses.
evidence: brackets containing an expression followed by

cases.question: How do you create an empty set?
cases.expected_answer: With set(), not {}, because {} creates an empty dictionary.
evidence: to create an empty set you have to use

cases.question: What is a set in Python?
cases.expected_answer: An unordered collection with no duplicate elements.
evidence: unordered collection with no duplicate elements

cases.question: Which types can be used as dictionary keys?
cases.expected_answer: Any immutable type, such as strings and numbers; tuples only if they contain only strings, numbers or tuples. Lists cannot be keys.
evidence: which can be any immutable type

cases.question: How can you avoid a KeyError when reading a key that may not exist?
cases.expected_answer: Use the get() method, which returns None or a given default value.
evidence: use the get() method instead

cases.question: Which function gives both the index and the value when looping over a sequence?
cases.expected_answer: enumerate().
evidence: at the same time using the enumerate() function

cases.question: How do tuples differ from lists?
cases.expected_answer: Tuples are immutable and usually hold a heterogeneous sequence accessed by unpacking or indexing; lists are mutable and usually homogeneous, accessed by iterating.
evidence: immutable, and usually contain a heterogeneous sequence

cases.question: What does it mean that and and or are short-circuit operators?
cases.expected_answer: Their arguments are evaluated from left to right and evaluation stops as soon as the outcome is determined.
evidence: evaluation stops as soon as the outcome is determined

cases.question: What ordering is used to compare two sequences of the same type?
cases.expected_answer: Lexicographical ordering.
evidence: the comparison uses lexicographical ordering
